## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Neil_Young&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

### Early career (1963–1966)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Neil_Young&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Early career (1963–1966)")]

Young and his mother settled in the working-class area of [Fort Rouge, Winnipeg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Rouge,_Winnipeg "Fort Rouge, Winnipeg"), where he enrolled in Earl Grey Junior High School. It was there that he formed his first band, the Jades, and met [Ken Koblun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Koblun "Ken Koblun"). While attending [Kelvin High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelvin_High_School "Kelvin High School") in Winnipeg, he played in several instrumental rock bands, eventually dropping out of school in favor of a musical career.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonough2002103-34) Young's first stable band was [the Squires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Squires "The Squires"), with Ken Koblun, Jeff Wuckert and Bill Edmondson on drums, who had a local hit called "The Sultan". Over three years, the band played hundreds of shows at community centers, dance halls, clubs and schools in Winnipeg and other parts of Manitoba. The band also played in [Fort William](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_William,_Ontario "Fort William, Ontario") (now part of the city of [Thunder Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thunder_Bay "Thunder Bay"), Ontario), where they recorded a series of demos produced by a local producer, Ray Dee, whom Young called "the original Briggs", referring to his later producer David Briggs.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonough2002105-35) While playing at The Flamingo, Young met [Stephen Stills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Stills "Stephen Stills"), whose band [the Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Company_(folk_rock_band) "The Company (folk rock band)") was playing at the same venue, and they became friends.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-36) The Squires primarily performed in Winnipeg and rural Manitoba in towns such as [Selkirk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selkirk,_Manitoba "Selkirk, Manitoba"), [Neepawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neepawa,_Manitoba "Neepawa, Manitoba"), [Brandon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brandon,_Manitoba "Brandon, Manitoba") and Giroux (near [Steinbach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steinbach,_Manitoba "Steinbach, Manitoba")), with a few shows in northern Ontario.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-37)

After leaving the Squires, Young worked in folk clubs in Winnipeg, where he first met [Joni Mitchell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joni_Mitchell "Joni Mitchell").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonough200296-38) Mitchell recalls Young as having been highly influenced by [Bob Dylan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Dylan "Bob Dylan") at the time.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-39) Young said [Phil Ochs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Ochs "Phil Ochs") was "a big influence on me", telling a radio station in 1969 that Ochs was "on the same level with Dylan in my eyes."[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonough2002137-40) Here he wrote some of his earliest and most enduring folk songs such as "[Sugar Mountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugar_Mountain_(song) "Sugar Mountain (song)")", about lost youth. Mitchell wrote "[The Circle Game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Circle_Game_(song) "The Circle Game (song)")" in response.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-41) The Winnipeg band [the Guess Who](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Guess_Who "The Guess Who") (with [Randy Bachman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Bachman "Randy Bachman") as lead guitarist) had a Canadian Top 40 hit with Young's "Flying on the Ground is Wrong", which was Young's first major success as a songwriter.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-42)

In 1965, Young toured Canada as a solo artist. In 1966, while in Toronto, he joined the [Rick James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_James "Rick James")-fronted [Mynah Birds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mynah_Birds "Mynah Birds"). The band managed to secure a record deal with the [Motown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motown "Motown") label, but as their first album was being recorded, James was arrested for being [AWOL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desertion "Desertion") from the Navy Reserve.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonough2002139-43) After the Mynah Birds disbanded, Young and the bass player [Bruce Palmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruce_Palmer "Bruce Palmer") decided to pawn the group's musical equipment and buy a [Pontiac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontiac_(automobile) "Pontiac (automobile)")[hearse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hearse "Hearse"), which they used to relocate to Los Angeles.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-WFP-44) Young admitted in a 1975 interview that he was in the United States illegally until he received a "green card" ([permanent residency permit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permanent_residence_(United_States) "Permanent residence (United States)")) in 1970.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-interview-45)

### Buffalo Springfield (1966–1968)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Neil_Young&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Buffalo Springfield (1966–1968)")]

Main article: [Buffalo Springfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buffalo_Springfield "Buffalo Springfield")

Once they reached Los Angeles, Young and Palmer met up with [Stephen Stills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Stills "Stephen Stills") and [Richie Furay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richie_Furay "Richie Furay") after a chance encounter in traffic on [Sunset Boulevard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunset_Boulevard "Sunset Boulevard").[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-WFP-44) Along with [Dewey Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dewey_Martin_(musician) "Dewey Martin (musician)"), they formed [Buffalo Springfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buffalo_Springfield "Buffalo Springfield"). A mixture of folk, country, [psychedelia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychedelia "Psychedelia"), and rock, lent a hard edge by the twin lead guitars of Stills and Young, made Buffalo Springfield a critical success, and their first record, _[Buffalo Springfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buffalo\_Springfield\_(album) "Buffalo Springfield (album)")_ (1966), sold well after Stills' topical song "[For What It's Worth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/For_What_It's_Worth "For What It's Worth")" became a hit, aided by Young's melodic harmonics played on electric guitar. According to _Rolling Stone_, the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame and other sources, Buffalo Springfield helped create the genres of folk rock and country rock.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-rollingstone-46)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-Unterberger-47)

Distrust of their management, as well as the arrest and deportation of Palmer, worsened the already strained relations among the group members and led to Buffalo Springfield's demise. A second album, _[Buffalo Springfield Again](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buffalo\_Springfield\_Again "Buffalo Springfield Again")_, was released in late 1967, but two of Young's three contributions were solo tracks recorded apart from the rest of the group. From that album, "[Mr. Soul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mr._Soul "Mr. Soul")" was the only Young song of the three that all five members of the group performed together.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-48)

In May 1968, the band split up for good, but to fulfill a contractual obligation, a final studio album, _[Last Time Around](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last\_Time\_Around "Last Time Around")_, was released. Young contributed the songs "On the Way Home" and "I Am a Child", singing lead on the latter.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-49)

In 1997, the band was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame; Young did not appear at the ceremony, writing in a letter to the Hall that their presentation, which was aired on [VH1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VH1 "VH1"), "has nothing to do with the spirit of Rock and Roll. It has everything to do with making money."[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-50)

Young played as a studio session guitarist for some 1968 recordings by [The Monkees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Monkees "The Monkees") which appeared on the _[Head](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head\_(The\_Monkees\_album) "Head (The Monkees album)")_ and _[Instant Replay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instant\_Replay\_(The\_Monkees\_album) "Instant Replay (The Monkees album)")_ albums.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-51)

### Going solo, Crazy Horse (1968–1969)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Neil_Young&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Going solo, Crazy Horse (1968–1969)")]

Main article: [Crazy Horse (band)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crazy_Horse_(band) "Crazy Horse (band)")

After the breakup of Buffalo Springfield, Young signed a solo deal with [Reprise Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reprise_Records "Reprise Records"), home of his colleague and friend [Joni Mitchell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joni_Mitchell "Joni Mitchell"), with whom he shared a manager, [Elliot Roberts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliot_Roberts "Elliot Roberts"). Roberts managed Young until Roberts' death in 2019. Young and Roberts immediately began work on Young's first solo record, _[Neil Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil\_Young\_(album) "Neil Young (album)")_ (January 22, 1969),[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-52) which received mixed reviews. In a 1970 interview,[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-53) Young deprecated the album as being "overdubbed rather than played".

For his next album, Young recruited three musicians from a band called the Rockets: [Danny Whitten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danny_Whitten "Danny Whitten") on guitar, [Billy Talbot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Talbot "Billy Talbot") on bass guitar, and [Ralph Molina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Molina "Ralph Molina") on drums. These three took the name [Crazy Horse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crazy_Horse_(band) "Crazy Horse (band)") (after [the historical figure of the same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crazy_Horse "Crazy Horse")), and _[Everybody Knows This Is Nowhere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everybody\_Knows\_This\_Is\_Nowhere "Everybody Knows This Is Nowhere")_ (May 1969) is credited to "Neil Young with Crazy Horse". Recorded in just two weeks, the album includes "[Cinnamon Girl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinnamon_Girl "Cinnamon Girl")", "[Cowgirl in the Sand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cowgirl_in_the_Sand "Cowgirl in the Sand")", and "[Down by the River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Down_by_the_River_(Neil_Young_song) "Down by the River (Neil Young song)")". Young reportedly wrote all three songs in bed on the same day while nursing a high fever of 39°C (102°F).[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-54)

### Crosby, Stills, Nash, and Young (1969–1970)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Neil_Young&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Crosby, Stills, Nash, and Young (1969–1970)")]

Main article: [Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crosby,_Stills,_Nash_&_Young "Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young")

Shortly after the release of _Everybody Knows This Is Nowhere,_ Young reunited with Stephen Stills by joining [Crosby, Stills & Nash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crosby,_Stills_&_Nash "Crosby, Stills & Nash"), who had already released one album, _[Crosby, Stills & Nash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crosby,\_Stills\_&\_Nash\_(album) "Crosby, Stills & Nash (album)")_, as a trio in May 1969. Young was originally offered a position as a sideman but agreed to join only if he received full membership, and the group – winners of the 1969 [Best New Artist Grammy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_New_Artist "Grammy Award for Best New Artist") – was renamed [Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crosby,_Stills,_Nash_&_Young "Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young").[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonough2002313-55) The quartet debuted in Chicago on August 16, 1969, and later performed at the famous [Woodstock Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodstock_Festival "Woodstock Festival"), during which Young skipped the majority of the acoustic set and refused to be filmed during the electric set, even telling the cameramen: "One of you fuckin' guys comes near me and I'm gonna fuckin' hit you with my guitar".[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonough2002318%E2%80%93320-56) During the making of their first album, _[Déjà Vu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%C3%A9j%C3%A0\_Vu\_(Crosby,\_Stills,\_Nash\_&\_Young\_album) "Déjà Vu (Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young album)")_ (March 11, 1970), the musicians frequently argued, particularly Young and Stills, who both fought for control. Stills continued throughout their lifelong relationship to criticize Young, saying that he "wanted to play folk music in a rock band".[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonough2002324-57)

Young wrote "[Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_(CSNY_song) "Ohio (CSNY song)")" after the [Kent State massacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_State_massacre "Kent State massacre") on May 4, 1970. CSNY quickly recorded the song and released it as a single, even as CSNY's "Teach Your Children" was still climbing the singles charts.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-58)

### _After the Gold Rush_, acoustic tour and _Harvest_ (1970–1972)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Neil_Young&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: After the Gold Rush, acoustic tour and Harvest (1970–1972)")]

Later in the year, Young released his third solo album, _[After the Gold Rush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/After\_the\_Gold\_Rush "After the Gold Rush")_ (August 31, 1970), which featured, among others, [Nils Lofgren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nils_Lofgren "Nils Lofgren"), [Stephen Stills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Stills "Stephen Stills"), and CSNY bassist [Greg Reeves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greg_Reeves "Greg Reeves"). Young also recorded some tracks with Crazy Horse, but dismissed them early in the sessions. The eventual recording was less amplified than _Everybody Knows This is Nowhere_, with a wider range of sounds. Young's newfound fame with CSNY made the album his commercial breakthrough as a solo artist, and it contains some of his best-known work, including "[Tell Me Why](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tell_Me_Why_(Neil_Young_song) "Tell Me Why (Neil Young song)")" and "[Don't Let It Bring You Down](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don't_Let_It_Bring_You_Down_(Neil_Young_song) "Don't Let It Bring You Down (Neil Young song)")"; the singles "[Only Love Can Break Your Heart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Only_Love_Can_Break_Your_Heart "Only Love Can Break Your Heart")" and "[When You Dance I Can Really Love](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/When_You_Dance_I_Can_Really_Love "When You Dance I Can Really Love")"; and the title track, "[After the Gold Rush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/After_the_Gold_Rush_(song) "After the Gold Rush (song)")", played on piano, with dreamlike lyrics that ran a gamut of subjects from drugs and interpersonal relationships to [environmental concerns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environmentalism "Environmentalism"). Young's bitter condemnation of racism in the heavy blues-rock song "[Southern Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Man_(song) "Southern Man (song)")" (along with a later song entitled "Alabama") was also controversial with southerners in an era of desegregation, prompting [Lynyrd Skynyrd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lynyrd_Skynyrd "Lynyrd Skynyrd") to decry Young by name in the lyrics to their hit "[Sweet Home Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweet_Home_Alabama_(song) "Sweet Home Alabama (song)")". However, Young said he was a fan of Skynyrd's music, and the band's front man [Ronnie Van Zant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronnie_Van_Zant "Ronnie Van Zant") was later photographed wearing a _[Tonight's the Night](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tonight's\_the\_Night\_(Neil\_Young\_album) "Tonight's the Night (Neil Young album)")_ T-shirt on the cover of [an album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Street_Survivors "Street Survivors").[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-59)

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/35/Neil_Young-early_promo.jpg/250px-Neil_Young-early_promo.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Neil_Young-early_promo.jpg)

Young in the 1970s

In the autumn of 1970, Young began a solo acoustic tour of North America, during which he played a variety of his Buffalo Springfield and CSNY songs on guitar and piano, along with material from his solo albums and several new songs. Some songs premiered by Young on the tour, like "Journey through the Past", would never find a home on a studio album, while other songs, like "See the Sky About to Rain", would only be released in coming years. Many gigs were sold out, including concerts at [Carnegie Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Hall "Carnegie Hall") and a pair of acclaimed hometown shows at Toronto's [Massey Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massey_Hall "Massey Hall"), which were taped for a planned live album. The shows became legendary among Young fans, with _[Live at Massey Hall 1971](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live\_at\_Massey\_Hall\_1971 "Live at Massey Hall 1971")_ being released in 2007, and other shows as official bootlegs in 2021 and 2022, as a part of Young's [Archive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young_Archives "Neil Young Archives") series.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-60)

Near the end of his tour, Young performed one of the new acoustic songs on the _[Johnny Cash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Johnny\_Cash\_Show\_(TV\_series) "The Johnny Cash Show (TV series)")_ TV show. "[The Needle and the Damage Done](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Needle_and_the_Damage_Done "The Needle and the Damage Done")", a somber lament on the pain caused by [heroin addiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heroin_addiction "Heroin addiction"), had been inspired in part by Crazy Horse member [Danny Whitten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danny_Whitten "Danny Whitten"), who eventually died while battling his drug problems.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilliamson200242-61)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaylor2006279-62) While in Nashville for the Cash taping, Young accepted the invitation of [Quadrafonic Sound Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadrafonic_Sound_Studios "Quadrafonic Sound Studios") owner [Elliot Mazer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliot_Mazer "Elliot Mazer") to record tracks there with a group of country-music session musicians who were pulled together at the last minute. Making a connection with them, he christened them [The Stray Gators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Stray_Gators "The Stray Gators"), and began playing with them. Befitting the immediacy of the project, [Linda Ronstadt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linda_Ronstadt "Linda Ronstadt") and [James Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Taylor "James Taylor") were brought in from the Cash taping to do background vocals. Against the advice of his producer [David Briggs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Briggs_(producer) "David Briggs (producer)"), he scrapped plans for the imminent release[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-63) of the live acoustic recording in favor of a studio album consisting of the Nashville sessions, electric-guitar oriented sessions recorded later in his barn, and two recordings made with the [London Symphony Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Symphony_Orchestra "London Symphony Orchestra") at Barking (credited as Barking Town Hall and now the [Broadway Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Broadway_(theatre) "The Broadway (theatre)")) during March 1971.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-64) The result was Young's fourth album, _[Harvest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvest\_(Neil\_Young\_album) "Harvest (Neil Young album)")_ (February 15, 1972), which was also the best selling album of 1972 in the US.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-65)

After his success with CSNY, Young purchased a ranch in the rural hills above Woodside and Redwood City in Northern California ("Broken Arrow Ranch", where he lived until his divorce in 2014).[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-rollingstone.com-66) He wrote the song "[Old Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Man_(song) "Old Man (song)")" in honor of the land's longtime caretaker, Louis Avila. The song "[A Man Needs a Maid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Man_Needs_a_Maid_(song) "A Man Needs a Maid (song)")" was inspired by his relationship with actress [Carrie Snodgress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carrie_Snodgress "Carrie Snodgress"). "[Heart of Gold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heart_of_Gold_(Neil_Young_song) "Heart of Gold (Neil Young song)")" was released as the first single from _Harvest_, the only No.1 hit in his career.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-whitburn_Top40-67) "Old Man" was also popular, reaching No. 31 on the _Billboard_ Hot 100 chart, marking Young's third and final appearance in the chart's Top 40 as a solo artist.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-whitburn_Top40-67)

The album's recording had been almost accidental. Its mainstream success caught Young off guard, and his first instinct was to back away from stardom. In the _[Decade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decade\_(Neil\_Young\_album) "Decade (Neil Young album)")_ (1977) compilation, Young chose to include his greatest hits from the period, but his handwritten liner notes famously described "Heart of Gold" as the song that "put me in the middle of the road. Traveling there soon became a bore, so I headed for the ditch. A rougher ride but I saw more interesting people there."[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-68)

### The "Ditch" Trilogy and personal struggles (1972–1974)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Neil_Young&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: The \"Ditch\" Trilogy and personal struggles (1972–1974)")]

Although a new tour with The Stray Gators (now augmented by Danny Whitten) had been planned to follow up on the success of _Harvest_, it became apparent during rehearsals that Whitten could not function due to drug abuse. On November 18, 1972, shortly after he was fired from the tour preparations, Whitten was found dead of an apparent alcohol/[diazepam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diazepam "Diazepam") overdose. Young described the incident to _Rolling Stone_'s [Cameron Crowe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cameron_Crowe "Cameron Crowe") in 1975: "[We] were rehearsing with him and he just couldn't cut it. He couldn't remember anything. He was too out of it. Too far gone. I had to tell him to go back to L.A. 'It's not happening, man. You're not together enough.' He just said, 'I've got nowhere else to go, man. How am I gonna tell my friends?' And he split. That night the coroner called me from L.A. and told me he'd OD'd. That blew my mind. I loved Danny. I felt responsible. And from there, I had to go right out on this huge tour of huge arenas. I was very nervous and ... insecure."[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-interview-45)

On the tour, Young struggled with his voice and the performance of drummer [Kenny Buttrey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenny_Buttrey "Kenny Buttrey"), a noted Nashville session musician who was unaccustomed to performing in the [hard rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock "Hard rock") milieu; Buttrey was eventually replaced by former CSNY drummer [Johnny Barbata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_Barbata "Johnny Barbata"), while [David Crosby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Crosby "David Crosby") and [Graham Nash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graham_Nash "Graham Nash") contributed rhythm guitar and backing vocals to the final dates of the tour. Young has often said the album assembled in the aftermath, _[Time Fades Away](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time\_Fades\_Away "Time Fades Away")_ (October 15, 1973), was his least favorite. It was not officially released on CD until 2017 (as part of Young's [Official Release Series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young_Archives#Official_Release_Series_05: "Neil Young Archives")). Nevertheless, Young and his band tried several new musical approaches in this period. _Time Fades Away_ was recorded live, although it was an album of new material, an approach Young would repeat with more success later on. _Time_ was the first of three consecutive commercial failures which became known collectively to fans as the "Ditch Trilogy", as contrasted with the more middle-of-the-road pop of _Harvest_.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-UnCut-69)

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fd/Neil_Young_in_Austin%2C_1976.jpg/250px-Neil_Young_in_Austin%2C_1976.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Neil_Young_in_Austin,_1976.jpg)

Young in [Austin, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin,_Texas "Austin, Texas"), on November 9, 1976

In the second half of 1973, Young formed The Santa Monica Flyers, with Crazy Horse's rhythm section augmented by [Nils Lofgren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nils_Lofgren "Nils Lofgren") on guitar and piano and _Harvest_/_Time Fades Away_ veteran [Ben Keith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Keith "Ben Keith") on pedal steel guitar. Deeply affected by the drug-induced deaths of Whitten and [roadie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roadie "Roadie")[Bruce Berry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruce_Berry_(roadie) "Bruce Berry (roadie)"), Young recorded an album specifically inspired by the incidents, _[Tonight's the Night](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tonight's\_the\_Night\_(Neil\_Young\_album) "Tonight's the Night (Neil Young album)")_ (June 20, 1975). The album's dark tone and rawness led Reprise to delay its release and Young had to pressure them for two years before they would do so.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonough2002430-70) While his record company was stalling, Young recorded another album, _[On the Beach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On\_the\_Beach\_(Neil\_Young\_album) "On the Beach (Neil Young album)")_ (July 16, 1974), which presented a more melodic, acoustic sound at times, including a recording of the older song "See the Sky About to Rain", but dealt with similarly dark themes such as the collapse of 1960s folk ideals, the downside of success and the underbelly of the Californian lifestyle. Like _Time Fades Away_, it sold poorly but eventually became a critical favorite, presenting some of Young's most original work. A review of the 2003 re-release on CD of _On the Beach_ described the music as "mesmerizing, harrowing, lucid, and bleary".[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-sven-71)

After completing _On the Beach_, Young reunited with _Harvest_ producer Elliot Mazer to record another acoustic album, _[Homegrown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homegrown\_(Neil\_Young\_album) "Homegrown (Neil Young album)")_. Most of the songs were written after Young's breakup with Carrie Snodgress, and thus the tone of the album was somewhat dark. Though _Homegrown_ was reportedly entirely complete, Young decided, not for the first or last time in his career, to drop it and release something else instead, in this case, _Tonight's the Night_, at the suggestion of [Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Band "The Band") bassist [Rick Danko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Danko "Rick Danko").[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonough2002469-72) Young further explained his move by saying: "It was a little too personal ... it scared me".[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonough2002469-72) Most of the songs from _Homegrown_ were later incorporated into other Young albums while the original album was not released until 2020. _Tonight's the Night,_ when finally released in 1975, sold poorly, as had the previous albums of the "ditch" trilogy, and received mixed reviews at the time, but is now regarded as a landmark album. In Young's own opinion, it was the closest he ever came to art.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonough2002433-73)

### Reunions, retrospectives and _Rust Never Sleeps_ (1974–1979)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Neil_Young&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Reunions, retrospectives and Rust Never Sleeps (1974–1979)")]

Young reunited with [Crosby, Stills, and Nash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crosby,_Stills,_and_Nash "Crosby, Stills, and Nash") after a four-year hiatus in the summer of 1974 for a concert tour that was partially recorded; highlights were ultimately released in 2014 as _[CSNY 1974](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CSNY\_1974 "CSNY 1974")_. It was one of the first ever stadium tours and the largest tour in which Young has participated to date.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonough2002452-74)

In 1975, Young reformed Crazy Horse with [Frank Sampedro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Sampedro "Frank Sampedro") on guitar as his backup band for his eighth album, _[Zuma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zuma\_(Neil\_Young\_&\_Crazy\_Horse\_album) "Zuma (Neil Young & Crazy Horse album)")_ (November 10, 1975). Many of the songs dealt with the theme of failed relationships; "[Cortez the Killer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cortez_the_Killer "Cortez the Killer")", a retelling of the [Spanish conquest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_conquest "Spanish conquest") of Mexico from the viewpoint of the [Aztecs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aztec "Aztec"), may also be heard as an allegory of love lost. _Zuma_'s closing track, "Through My Sails", was the only released fragment from aborted sessions with Crosby, Stills and Nash for another group album.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-75)

In 1976, Young reunited with Stephen Stills for the album _[Long May You Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long\_May\_You\_Run "Long May You Run")_ (September 20, 1976), credited to [The Stills-Young Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Stills-Young_Band "The Stills-Young Band"); the follow-up tour was ended midway through by Young, who sent Stills a [telegram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegram "Telegram") that read: "Funny how some things that start spontaneously end that way. Eat a peach, Neil."[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonough2002502-76)

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/56/The_Last_Waltz.jpg/250px-The_Last_Waltz.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Last_Waltz.jpg)

_The Last Waltz_, Young (center on left microphone) performing with Bob Dylan and [The Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Band "The Band"), among others in 1976

In 1976, Young performed with Bob Dylan, Joni Mitchell, and numerous other rock musicians in the high-profile all-star concert _[The Last Waltz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Last\_Waltz "The Last Waltz")_, the final performance by [The Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Band "The Band"). The release of [Martin Scorsese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Scorsese "Martin Scorsese")'s movie of the concert was delayed while Scorsese unwillingly re-edited it to obscure the lump of cocaine that was clearly visible hanging from Young's nose during his performance of "[Helpless](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helpless_(Crosby,_Stills,_Nash_&_Young_song) "Helpless (Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young song)")".[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-Exclaim-77)_[American Stars 'n Bars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American\_Stars\_'n\_Bars "American Stars 'n Bars")_ (June 13, 1977) contained two songs originally recorded for the _Homegrown_ album, "Homegrown" and "Star of Bethlehem", as well as newer material, including the future concert staple "[Like a Hurricane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Like_a_Hurricane_(Neil_Young_song) "Like a Hurricane (Neil Young song)")". Performers on the record included [Linda Ronstadt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linda_Ronstadt "Linda Ronstadt"), [Emmylou Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmylou_Harris "Emmylou Harris") and Young protégé [Nicolette Larson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolette_Larson "Nicolette Larson") along with Crazy Horse. In 1977, Young also released the compilation _[Decade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decade\_(Neil\_Young\_album) "Decade (Neil Young album)")_, a personally selected set of songs spanning every aspect of his work, including a handful of previously unreleased songs. The record included less commercial album tracks alongside radio hits.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-78)

In June 1977 Young joined with Jeff Blackburn, Bob Mosley and John Craviotto (who later founded [Craviotto drums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craviotto_drums "Craviotto drums")) to form a band called The Ducks. Over seven-week the band performed 22 shows in Santa Cruz CA but were not allowed to appear beyond city limits due to Young's Crazy Horse contract. In April 2023 Young officially released a double album of songs culled from the band's performances at multiple venues as well as from sessions at a local recording studio. The double album was part of the Neil Young Archives project positioned within the Official Bootleg Series, titled High Flyin'.

_[Comes a Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comes\_a\_Time "Comes a Time")_ (October 2, 1978), Young's first entirely new solo recording since the mid-1970s, marked a return to the commercially accessible, Nashville-inspired sound of _Harvest_ while also featuring contributions from Larson and Crazy Horse. The album also marked a return to his folk roots, as exemplified by a cover of [Ian Tyson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Tyson "Ian Tyson")'s "[Four Strong Winds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_Strong_Winds "Four Strong Winds")", a song Young associated with his childhood in Canada. Another of the album's songs, "[Lotta Love](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lotta_Love "Lotta Love")", was also recorded by Larson, with her version reaching No. 8 on the _Billboard_ Hot 100 in February 1979. In 1978, much of the filming was done for Young's film _[Human Highway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human\_Highway "Human Highway")_, which took its name from a song featured on _Comes a Time_. Over four years, Young would spend US$3,000,000 of his own money on production (US$14,808,673 in 2025 dollars[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-inflation-US-79)). This also marked the beginning of his brief collaboration with the [art punk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_punk "Art punk") band [Devo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Devo "Devo"), whose members appeared in the film.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonough2002575%E2%80%93577-80)

Young set out in 1978 on the lengthy _Rust Never Sleeps_ tour, in which he played a wealth of new material. Each concert was divided into a solo acoustic set and an electric set with Crazy Horse. The electric sets, featuring an abrasive style of playing, were influenced by the [punk rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punk_rock "Punk rock")[zeitgeist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeitgeist "Zeitgeist") of the late 1970s and provided a stark contrast from _Comes a Time_.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonough2002529%E2%80%93537-81) Two new songs, the acoustic "[My My, Hey Hey (Out of the Blue)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My_My,_Hey_Hey_(Out_of_the_Blue) "My My, Hey Hey (Out of the Blue)")" and electric "[Hey Hey, My My (Into the Black)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey_Hey,_My_My_(Into_the_Black) "Hey Hey, My My (Into the Black)")" were the centerpiece of the new material. During the filming of _Human Highway_, Young had collaborated with Devo on a cacophonous version of "Hey Hey, My My" at the [Different Fur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Different_Fur "Different Fur") studio in San Francisco and would later introduce the song to Crazy Horse.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonough2002531%E2%80%93532-82) The lyric "It's better to burn out than to fade away" was widely quoted by his peers and critics.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonough2002531%E2%80%93532-82) The album has also widely been considered a precursor of [grunge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grunge "Grunge") music with the bands [Nirvana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nirvana_(band) "Nirvana (band)") and [Pearl Jam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearl_Jam "Pearl Jam") having cited Young's heavily distorted and abrasive guitar style on the B side to this album as an inspiration. Young also compared the rise of [Johnny Rotten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_Rotten "Johnny Rotten") with that of the recently deceased "King" [Elvis Presley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elvis_Presley "Elvis Presley"), who himself had once been disparaged as a dangerous influence only to later become an [icon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_icon "Pop icon"). Rotten returned the favor by playing one of Young's songs, "Revolution Blues" from _[On the Beach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On\_the\_Beach\_(Neil\_Young\_album) "On the Beach (Neil Young album)")_, on a London radio show, an early sign of Young's eventual embrace by several punk-influenced alternative musicians.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-83)

Young's two accompanying albums _[Rust Never Sleeps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rust\_Never\_Sleeps "Rust Never Sleeps")_ (July 2, 1979; new material culled from live recordings, but featuring studio overdubs) and _[Live Rust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live\_Rust "Live Rust")_ (November 19, 1979; a genuine concert recording featuring old and new material) captured the two sides of the concerts, with solo acoustic songs on side A, and fierce, uptempo, electric songs on side B. A movie version of the concerts, also called _Rust Never Sleeps_ (1979), was directed by Young under the pseudonym "Bernard Shakey". Young worked with rock artist [Jim Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Evans_(artist) "Jim Evans (artist)") to create the poster art for the film, using the _[Star Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star\_Wars "Star Wars")_[Jawas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jawas "Jawas") as a theme. Young's work since _Harvest_ had alternated between being rejected by mass audiences and being seen as backward-looking by critics, sometimes both at once, and now he was suddenly viewed as relevant by a new generation, who began to discover his earlier work. Readers and critics of _Rolling Stone_ voted him Artist of the Year for 1979 (along with [The Who](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Who "The Who")), selected _[Rust Never Sleeps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rust\_Never\_Sleeps "Rust Never Sleeps")_ as Album of the Year, and voted him Male Vocalist of the Year as well.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-84)_[The Village Voice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Village\_Voice "The Village Voice")_ named _Rust Never Sleeps_ as the year's second best album in the [Pazz & Jop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pazz_&_Jop "Pazz & Jop") Poll,[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-85) a survey of nationwide critics, and honored Young as the Artist of the Decade.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-86)

### Experimental years (1980–1988)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Neil_Young&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Experimental years (1980–1988)")]

After providing the incidental music to the 1980 film _[Where the Buffalo Roam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Where\_the\_Buffalo\_Roam "Where the Buffalo Roam")_, Young released _[Hawks & Doves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawks\_&\_Doves "Hawks & Doves")_ (November 3, 1980), a short record pieced together from sessions going back to 1974.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-Hawks_&_Doves_Review-87)

_[Re·ac·tor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Re%C2%B7ac%C2%B7tor "Re·ac·tor")_ (1981), an electric album recorded with Crazy Horse, also included material from the 1970s.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-88) Young did not tour in support of either album; in total, he played only two shows, a set at the 1980 Bread and Roses Festival in [Berkeley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berkeley,_California "Berkeley, California")[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-89) and another at the Mike Bloomfield Tribute at The Ritz,[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-90) between the end of his 1978 tour with Crazy Horse and the start of his tour with the Trans Band in mid-1982.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-91)

> The 80s were really good. The 80s were like, artistically, very strong for me, because I knew no boundaries and was experimenting with everything that I could come across, sometimes with great success, sometimes with terrible results, but nonetheless I was able to do this, and I was able to realize that I wasn't in a box, and I wanted to establish that.

—Neil Young[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-92)

The 1982 album _[Trans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trans\_(album) "Trans (album)")_, which incorporated [vocoders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vocoder "Vocoder"), synthesizers, and electronic beats, was Young's first for the new label [Geffen Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geffen_Records "Geffen Records") (distributed at the time by [Warner Bros. Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Bros._Records "Warner Bros. Records"), whose parent [Warner Music Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Music_Group "Warner Music Group") owns most of Young's solo and band catalog) and represented a distinct stylistic departure. Young later revealed that an inspiration for the album was the theme of technology and communication with his son, who could not speak.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-93) An extensive tour preceded the release of the album and was documented by the video _[Neil Young in Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil\_Young\_in\_Berlin "Neil Young in Berlin")_, which saw release in 1986.

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2e/Para_Rael99_%28que_nos_quiten_lo_bailao%29.jpg/250px-Para_Rael99_%28que_nos_quiten_lo_bailao%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Para_Rael99_(que_nos_quiten_lo_bailao).jpg)

Young playing in [Barcelona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barcelona "Barcelona"), Spain, 1984

Young's next album, 1983's _[Everybody's Rockin'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everybody's\_Rockin' "Everybody's Rockin'")_, included several [rockabilly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockabilly "Rockabilly") covers and clocked in at less than 25 minutes in length. Young was backed by the Shocking Pinks for the supporting US tour. _Trans_ (1982) had already drawn the ire of label head [David Geffen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Geffen "David Geffen") for its lack of commercial appeal, and with _Everybody's Rockin_' following seven months later, Geffen Records sued Young for making music "unrepresentative" of himself.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-94) The album was also notable as the first for which Young made commercial music videos – [Tim Pope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Pope "Tim Pope") directed the videos for "Wonderin'" and "Cry, Cry, Cry". Also premiered in 1983, though little seen, was the long-gestating _Human Highway_. Co-directed and co-written by Young, the eclectic comedy starred Young, [Dean Stockwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dean_Stockwell "Dean Stockwell"), [Russ Tamblyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russ_Tamblyn "Russ Tamblyn"), [Dennis Hopper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dennis_Hopper "Dennis Hopper"), [David Blue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Blue_(musician) "David Blue (musician)"), [Sally Kirkland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sally_Kirkland "Sally Kirkland"), [Charlotte Stewart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlotte_Stewart "Charlotte Stewart") and members of Devo.

Young did not release an album in 1984, his first unproductive year since beginning his career with Buffalo Springfield in 1966. Young's lack of productivity was largely due to the ongoing legal battle with Geffen, although he was also frustrated that the label had rejected his 1983 country album _[Old Ways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old\_Ways "Old Ways")_.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-95) It was also the year when Young's third child was born, a girl named Amber Jean, who was later diagnosed with inherited [epilepsy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epilepsy "Epilepsy").[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-96)

Young spent most of 1984 and all of 1985 touring for _Old Ways_ (August 12, 1985) with his country band, the International Harvesters. The album was finally released in an altered form midway through 1985. Young also appeared at that year's [Live Aid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live_Aid "Live Aid") concert in [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia"), collaborating with Crosby, Stills and Nash for the quartet's first performance for a paying audience in over ten years.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-97)

Young's last two albums for Geffen were more conventional in the genre, although they incorporated production techniques like synthesizers and echoing drums that were previously uncommon in Young's music. Young recorded 1986's _[Landing on Water](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landing\_on\_Water "Landing on Water")_ without Crazy Horse but reunited with the band for the subsequent year-long tour and final Geffen album, _[Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life\_(1987\_album) "Life (1987 album)")_, which emerged in 1987. Young's album sales dwindled steadily throughout the eighties; today _Life_ remains his all-time-least successful studio album, with an estimated four hundred thousand sales worldwide.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-98)

Switching back to his old label Reprise Records, Young continued to tour relentlessly, assembling a new blues band called The Bluenotes in mid-1987 (a legal dispute with musician [Harold Melvin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Melvin "Harold Melvin") forced the eventual rechristening of the band as Ten Men Working midway through the tour). The addition of a [brass section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brass_section "Brass section") provided a new [jazzier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") sound, and the title track of 1988's _[This Note's For You](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/This\_Note's\_For\_You "This Note's For You")_ became Young's first hit single of the decade. Accompanied by a video that parodied corporate rock, the pretensions of advertising, and [Michael Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Jackson "Michael Jackson"), the song was initially unofficially banned by MTV for mentioning the brand names of some of their sponsors. Young wrote an open letter, "What does the M in MTV stand for: music or money?" Despite this, the video was eventually named [best video of the year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTV_Video_Music_Award_for_Best_Video_of_the_Year "MTV Video Music Award for Best Video of the Year") by the network in 1989.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonough200224%E2%80%9332-99)

Young reunited with Crosby, Stills, and Nash to record the 1988 album _[American Dream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American\_Dream\_(Crosby,\_Stills,\_Nash\_&\_Young\_album) "American Dream (Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young album)")_ and play two benefit concerts late in the year, but the group did not embark upon a full tour.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-100)

Young attracted criticism from liberals in the music industry when he supported [President Ronald Reagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_Ronald_Reagan "President Ronald Reagan") and said he was "tired of people constantly apologizing for being Americans".[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-101) In a 1985 interview with _[Melody Maker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melody\_Maker "Melody Maker")_, he said about the [AIDS pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIDS_pandemic "AIDS pandemic"): "You go to a supermarket and you see a faggot behind the fuckin' cash register, you don't want him to handle your potatoes."[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-Rolling_Stone-2013-102) In the same interview, Young also complained about [welfare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_programs_in_the_United_States "Social programs in the United States") beneficiaries, saying: "Stop being supported by the government and get out and work. You have to make the weak stand up on one leg, or half a leg, whatever they've got."[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-103)_[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling\_Stone "Rolling Stone")_ wrote in 2013 that Young "almost certainly regrets that horrific statement" and that he "quickly moved away from right-wing politics".[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-Rolling_Stone-2013-102)

Young took a turn at acting in 1988 by appearing in the Steven Kovacs film _['68](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/'68\_(film) "'68 (film)")_. He played the character Westy, a cranky owner of a motorcycle shop and a fan of Senator Joseph McCarthy.

### Return to prominence (1989–1999)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Neil_Young&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Return to prominence (1989–1999)")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/14/Neil_Young_1996.jpg/250px-Neil_Young_1996.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Neil_Young_1996.jpg)

Young performing in 1996 in [Turku](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turku "Turku"), Finland

Young's 1989 single "[Rockin' in the Free World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockin'_in_the_Free_World "Rockin' in the Free World")", which hit No.2 on the US mainstream-rock charts, and accompanied the album, _[Freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom\_(1989\_album) "Freedom (1989 album)")_, returned Young to the popular consciousness after a decade of sometimes-difficult genre experiments. The album's lyrics were often overtly political; "Rockin' in the Free World" deals with homelessness, terrorism, and environmental degradation, implicitly criticizing the government policies of President [George H. W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_H._W._Bush "George H. W. Bush").[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-104)

The use of heavy [feedback](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feedback "Feedback") and distortion on several _Freedom_ tracks was reminiscent of the _[Rust Never Sleeps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rust\_Never\_Sleeps "Rust Never Sleeps")_ (1979) album and foreshadowed the imminent rise of grunge. The rising stars of the subgenre, including [Nirvana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nirvana_(band) "Nirvana (band)")'s [Kurt Cobain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kurt_Cobain "Kurt Cobain") and [Pearl Jam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearl_Jam "Pearl Jam")'s [Eddie Vedder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_Vedder "Eddie Vedder"), frequently cited Young as a major influence, contributing to his popular revival. A tribute album called _[The Bridge: A Tribute to Neil Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Bridge:\_A\_Tribute\_to\_Neil\_Young "The Bridge: A Tribute to Neil Young")_ was released in 1989, featuring covers by a range of alternative and grunge acts, including [Sonic Youth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonic_Youth "Sonic Youth"), [Nick Cave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cave "Nick Cave"), [Soul Asylum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_Asylum "Soul Asylum"), [Dinosaur Jr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinosaur_Jr "Dinosaur Jr"), and the [Pixies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pixies_(band) "Pixies (band)").[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-105)

Young's 1990 album _[Ragged Glory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ragged\_Glory "Ragged Glory")_, recorded with Crazy Horse in a barn on his Northern California ranch, continued this distortion-heavy aesthetic. Young toured for the album with Orange County, California country-punk band [Social Distortion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_Distortion "Social Distortion") and Sonic Youth as support, much to the consternation of many of his old fans.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-sonic-106)_[Weld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weld\_(album) "Weld (album)")_, a two-disc live album documenting the tour, was released in 1991.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-sonic-106) Sonic Youth's influence was evident on _[Arc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arc\_(Neil\_Young\_&\_Crazy\_Horse\_album) "Arc (Neil Young & Crazy Horse album)")_, a 35-minute collage of feedback and distortion spliced together at the suggestion of [Thurston Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thurston_Moore "Thurston Moore") and originally packaged with some versions of _Weld_.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-sonic-106)

1992's _[Harvest Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvest\_Moon\_(album) "Harvest Moon (album)")_ marked an abrupt return (prompted by Young's [hyperacusis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperacusis "Hyperacusis") in the aftermath of the _Weld_ tour) to the country and folk-rock stylings of _Harvest_ and reunited him with some of the musicians from that album, including the core members of the Stray Gators and singers [Linda Ronstadt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linda_Ronstadt "Linda Ronstadt") and [James Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Taylor "James Taylor"). The title track was a minor hit, and the record was well received by critics, winning the [Juno Award for Album of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juno_Award_for_Album_of_the_Year "Juno Award for Album of the Year") in 1994. Young also contributed to lifelong friend [Randy Bachman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Bachman "Randy Bachman")'s nostalgic 1992 tune "Prairie Town", and garnered a 1993 [Academy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Song "Academy Award for Best Song") nomination for his song "Philadelphia", from the soundtrack of the [Jonathan Demme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Demme "Jonathan Demme") movie [of the same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia_(movie) "Philadelphia (movie)"). An _[MTV Unplugged](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unplugged\_(Neil\_Young\_album) "Unplugged (Neil Young album)")_ performance and album emerged in 1993. Later that year, Young collaborated with [Booker T. and the M.G.s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Booker_T._and_the_M.G.s "Booker T. and the M.G.s") for a summer tour of Europe and North America, with [Blues Traveler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blues_Traveler "Blues Traveler"), [Soundgarden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soundgarden "Soundgarden"), and [Pearl Jam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearl_Jam "Pearl Jam") also on the bill. Some European shows ended with a rendition of "Rockin' in the Free World" played with [Pearl Jam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearl_Jam "Pearl Jam"), foreshadowing their eventual full-scale collaboration two years later.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-107)

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/18/Neil_Young%2C_Heart_of_Gold.jpg/250px-Neil_Young%2C_Heart_of_Gold.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Neil_Young,_Heart_of_Gold.jpg)

Young on stage in [Barcelona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barcelona "Barcelona")

In 1994, Young again collaborated with Crazy Horse on _[Sleeps with Angels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleeps\_with\_Angels "Sleeps with Angels")_, a record whose dark, somber mood was influenced by [Kurt Cobain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kurt_Cobain "Kurt Cobain")'s death earlier that year: the title track in particular dealt with Cobain's life and death without mentioning him by name. Cobain had quoted Young's lyric "It's better to burn out than fade away" (a line from "[My My, Hey Hey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My_My,_Hey_Hey_(Out_of_the_Blue) "My My, Hey Hey (Out of the Blue)")") in [his suicide note](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_of_Kurt_Cobain#Suicide_note "Death of Kurt Cobain"). Young had reportedly made repeated attempts to contact Cobain before his death.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-108) Young and Pearl Jam performed "Act of Love" at an abortion rights benefit along with Crazy Horse, and were present at a Rock and Roll Hall of Fame dinner, sparking interest in a collaboration between the two.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-109) Still enamored with the grunge scene, Young reconnected with Pearl Jam in 1995 for the live-in-the-studio album _[Mirror Ball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mirror\_Ball\_(Neil\_Young\_album) "Mirror Ball (Neil Young album)")_ and a tour of Europe with the band and producer [Brendan O'Brien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brendan_O'Brien_(music_producer) "Brendan O'Brien (music producer)") backing Young. 1995 also marked Young's induction into the [Rock and Roll Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_and_Roll_Hall_of_Fame "Rock and Roll Hall of Fame"), where he was inducted by Eddie Vedder.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-rockhall.com-110)

> Young has consistently demonstrated the unbridled passion of an artist who understands that self-renewal is the only way to avoid burning out. For this reason, he has remained one of the most significant artists of the rock and roll era.

—[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_and_Roll_Hall_of_Fame "Rock and Roll Hall of Fame") website.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-rockhall.com-110)[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-R&R_Hall_of_Fame1-111)

In 1995, Young and his manager [Elliot Roberts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliot_Roberts "Elliot Roberts") founded a record label, Vapor Records.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-canadianmusichalloffame-112) It has released recordings by [Tegan and Sara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegan_and_Sara "Tegan and Sara"), [Spoon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spoon_(band) "Spoon (band)"), [Jonathan Richman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Richman "Jonathan Richman"), [Vic Chesnutt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vic_Chesnutt "Vic Chesnutt"), [Everest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everest_(band) "Everest (band)"), [Pegi Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pegi_Young "Pegi Young"), [Jets Overhead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jets_Overhead "Jets Overhead"), and Young himself, among others.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-canadianmusichalloffame-112)

Young's next collaborative partner was the filmmaker [Jim Jarmusch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Jarmusch "Jim Jarmusch"), who asked Young to compose [a soundtrack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead_Man_(soundtrack) "Dead Man (soundtrack)") to his 1995 black-and-white western film _[Dead Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead\_Man "Dead Man")_. Young's instrumental soundtrack was improvised while he watched the film alone in a studio. The death of longtime mentor, friend, and producer [David Briggs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Briggs_(producer) "David Briggs (producer)") in late 1995 prompted Young to reconnect with Crazy Horse the next year for the album and tour _[Broken Arrow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broken\_Arrow\_(album) "Broken Arrow (album)")_. A Jarmusch-directed concert film and live album of the tour, _[Year of the Horse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Year\_of\_the\_Horse\_(Neil\_Young\_album) "Year of the Horse (Neil Young album)")_, emerged in 1997. From 1996 to 1997, Young and Crazy Horse toured extensively throughout Europe and North America, including a stint as part of the [H.O.R.D.E.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H.O.R.D.E. "H.O.R.D.E.") Festival's sixth annual tour.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-113)

In 1998, Young renewed his collaboration with the rock band [Phish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phish "Phish"), sharing the stage at the annual [Farm Aid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farm_Aid "Farm Aid") concert and then at Young's Bridge School Benefit, where he joined headliners Phish for renditions of "[Helpless](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helpless_(Crosby,_Stills,_Nash_&_Young_song) "Helpless (Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young song)")" and "[I Shall Be Released](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Shall_Be_Released "I Shall Be Released")".[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-114) Phish declined Young's later invitation to be his backing band on his 1999 North American tour.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-115)

The decade ended with the release in late 1999 of _[Looking Forward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Looking\_Forward "Looking Forward")_, another reunion with Crosby, Stills, and Nash. The subsequent tour of the United States and Canada with the reformed quartet earned $42.1 million, making it the eighth largest grossing tour of 2000.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-116)

#### 2005 health issues

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Neil_Young&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: 2005 health issues")]

In March 2005, while working on the _[Prairie Wind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prairie\_Wind "Prairie Wind")_ album in [Nashville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nashville,_Tennessee "Nashville, Tennessee"),[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-Time-120) Young was diagnosed with a brain [aneurysm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aneurysm "Aneurysm"). He was treated successfully with a minimally invasive [neuroradiological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neuroradiology "Neuroradiology") procedure and performed in a New York hospital on March 29,[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-121) but passed out two days later on a New York street from bleeding from the [femoral artery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Femoral_artery "Femoral artery"), which radiologists had used to access the aneurysm.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-122) The complication forced Young to cancel his scheduled appearance at the [Juno Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juno_Awards "Juno Awards") telecast in Winnipeg, but within months he was back on stage, appearing at the close of the [Live 8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live_8 "Live 8") concert in [Barrie, Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barrie,_Ontario "Barrie, Ontario"), on July 2. During the performance, he debuted a new song, a soft hymn called "When God Made Me". Young's brush with death influenced _Prairie Wind_'s themes of retrospection and mortality.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-123)

The discography and filmography of Neil Young contains both albums and films produced by Young. Through his career most of Young's work has been recorded for and distributed by [Reprise Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reprise_Records "Reprise Records"), a company owned by [Warner Bros. Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Records "Warner Records") since 1963 and now part of the [Warner Music Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Music_Group "Warner Music Group"). The only exceptions are Young's five albums for [Geffen Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geffen_Records "Geffen Records") in the 1980s, which were once distributed by Warner, but are now distributed by [Universal Music Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Music_Group "Universal Music Group").

See also the [Archives Series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young_Archives "Neil Young Archives") listed separately below.

The discography and filmography of Neil Young contains both albums and films produced by Young. Through his career most of Young's work has been recorded for and distributed by [Reprise Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reprise_Records "Reprise Records"), a company owned by [Warner Bros. Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Records "Warner Records") since 1963 and now part of the [Warner Music Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Music_Group "Warner Music Group"). The only exceptions are Young's five albums for [Geffen Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geffen_Records "Geffen Records") in the 1980s, which were once distributed by Warner, but are now distributed by [Universal Music Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Music_Group "Universal Music Group").

Neil Young has included material recorded live on many of his albums; listed here are albums consisting completely or primarily of live concert recordings. _[Time Fades Away](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time\_Fades\_Away "Time Fades Away")_ consists of previously unreleased material. _[Weld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weld\_(album) "Weld (album)")_ and _[Arc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arc\_(Neil\_Young\_&\_Crazy\_Horse\_album) "Arc (Neil Young & Crazy Horse album)")_ were initially released as a single package, _Arc-Weld_. See also the [Archives Series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young_Archives "Neil Young Archives") listed separately below.

**Neil Percival Young**[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-gg.ca-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-OM-2) (born November 12, 1945) is a Canadian and American[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-3) singer-songwriter and musician. Son of journalist and author [Scott Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Young_(writer) "Scott Young (writer)"), Young embarked on a music career in [Winnipeg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winnipeg "Winnipeg") in the 1960s. He then moved to Los Angeles, forming the [folk rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_rock "Folk rock") group [Buffalo Springfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buffalo_Springfield "Buffalo Springfield"). His solo career, often backed by the band [Crazy Horse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crazy_Horse_(band) "Crazy Horse (band)"), includes critically acclaimed albums such as _[Everybody Knows This Is Nowhere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everybody\_Knows\_This\_Is\_Nowhere "Everybody Knows This Is Nowhere")_ (1969), _[After the Gold Rush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/After\_the\_Gold\_Rush "After the Gold Rush")_ (1970), _[Harvest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvest\_(Neil\_Young\_album) "Harvest (Neil Young album)")_ (1972), _[On the Beach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On\_the\_Beach\_(Neil\_Young\_album) "On the Beach (Neil Young album)")_ (1974), and _[Rust Never Sleeps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rust\_Never\_Sleeps "Rust Never Sleeps")_ (1979). Young was also a part-time member of [Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crosby,_Stills,_Nash_&_Young "Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young"), with whom he recorded the chart-topping 1970 album _[Déjà Vu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%C3%A9j%C3%A0\_Vu\_(Crosby,\_Stills,\_Nash\_&\_Young\_album) "Déjà Vu (Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young album)")_.

Young's deeply personal lyrics[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-Los_Angeles_Daily_News-1993-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-6) and signature high [tenor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenor "Tenor") singing voice[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-8) define his long career. He also plays piano and harmonica on many albums, which frequently combine [folk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_music "Folk music"), [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music"), [country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_music "Country music") and other musical genres. His often distorted electric guitar playing, especially with Crazy Horse, earned him the nickname "[Godfather](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honorific_nicknames_in_popular_music "Honorific nicknames in popular music") of [Grunge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grunge "Grunge")"[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEchard200543-9) and led to his 1995 album _[Mirror Ball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mirror\_Ball\_(Neil\_Young\_album) "Mirror Ball (Neil Young album)")_ with [Pearl Jam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearl_Jam "Pearl Jam"). More recently, he has been backed by [Promise of the Real](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lukas_Nelson_&_Promise_of_the_Real "Lukas Nelson & Promise of the Real").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-10)

Young directed (or co-directed) films using the pseudonym "Bernard Shakey", including _[Journey Through the Past](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journey\_Through\_the\_Past\_(film) "Journey Through the Past (film)")_ (1973), _[Rust Never Sleeps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rust\_Never\_Sleeps#Concert\_film "Rust Never Sleeps")_ (1979), _[Human Highway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human\_Highway "Human Highway")_ (1982), _Greendale_ (2003), _[CSNY/Déjà Vu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CSNY/D%C3%A9j%C3%A0\_Vu "CSNY/Déjà Vu")_ (2008), and _Harvest Time_ (2022). He also contributed to the soundtracks of the films _[Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia\_(film) "Philadelphia (film)")_ (1993) and _[Dead Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead\_Man "Dead Man")_ (1995).

Young has received multiple [Grammy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award "Grammy Award") and [Juno Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juno_Award "Juno Award"). The [Rock and Roll Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_and_Roll_Hall_of_Fame "Rock and Roll Hall of Fame") has inducted him twice: in 1995 as a solo artist and in 1997 as a member of Buffalo Springfield.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-11) In 2023, _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling\_Stone "Rolling Stone")_ magazine ranked Young No. 30 on its list of the "250 Greatest Guitarists of All Time".[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-12) Young is also on _Rolling Stone_'s [list of the 100 greatest musical artists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone's_100_Greatest_Artists_of_All_Time "Rolling Stone's 100 Greatest Artists of All Time"), and 21 of his albums and singles have been [certified gold or platinum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Certified_gold "Certified gold") in the U.S.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-13) Young was awarded the [Order of Manitoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_Manitoba "Order of Manitoba") in 2006[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-OM-2) and was made an Officer of the [Order of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_Canada "Order of Canada") in 2010.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-gg.ca-1)

## Early life (1945–1963)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Neil_Young&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life (1945–1963)")]

Neil Percival Young[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonough200237-14) was born on November 12, 1945, in [Toronto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto "Toronto"), Ontario.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-16) His mother, Edna Blow Ragland "Rassy" Young (1918–1990) was a member of the [Daughters of the American Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daughters_of_the_American_Revolution "Daughters of the American Revolution"),[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-17) while his father, [Scott Alexander Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Young_(writer) "Scott Young (writer)") (1918–2005), was a journalist and author.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-18) Although Canadian, Young's mother had American and French ancestry.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-FOOTNOTEYoung199716-19) His parents married in 1940 in [Winnipeg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winnipeg "Winnipeg"), Manitoba, and moved to Toronto shortly thereafter. There, the couple's first son, Robert "Bob" Young, was born in 1942.

Shortly after Young's birth, the family moved to rural [Omemee, Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omemee,_Ontario "Omemee, Ontario"), which he later described fondly as a "sleepy little place".[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonough200222%E2%80%9342-20) He contracted [polio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polio "Polio") in the late summer of 1951 during the last major outbreak of the disease in Ontario and, as a result, became partially paralyzed on his left side.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonough200244%E2%80%9346-21) After the conclusion of his hospitalization, the Young family wintered in Florida because they believed its mild weather would help Neil's convalescence.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonough200246-22) During that period, Young briefly attended Faulkner Elementary School in [New Smyrna Beach, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Smyrna_Beach,_Florida "New Smyrna Beach, Florida"). In 1952, upon returning to Canada, Young moved from Omemee to [Pickering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pickering,_Ontario "Pickering, Ontario") (1956) and then lived for a year in Winnipeg (where he would later return) before relocating to Toronto (1957–1960). While in Toronto, he briefly attended [Lawrence Park Collegiate Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_Park_Collegiate_Institute "Lawrence Park Collegiate Institute") as a first-year student in 1959.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-23) According to rumor, he was expelled for riding a motorcycle down the hall of the school.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-24) He also became interested in the popular music he heard on the radio.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonough200246%E2%80%9354-25)

When he was 12, his father, who had had several extramarital affairs, left his mother. She asked for a divorce, which was granted in 1960.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-26) She moved back to Winnipeg with Neil joining her there, while his brother, Bob, stayed with their father in Toronto.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonough200255%E2%80%9368-27)

During the mid-1950s, Young listened to [rock 'n roll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_and_roll "Rock and roll"), [rockabilly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockabilly "Rockabilly"), [doo-wop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doo-wop "Doo-wop"), [R&B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues"), [country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_music "Country music"), and western pop. He idolized [Elvis Presley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elvis_Presley "Elvis Presley") and later referred to him in a number of his songs.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-28) Other early musical influences included [Link Wray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Link_Wray "Link Wray"),[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-29)[Lonnie Mack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lonnie_Mack "Lonnie Mack"),[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-30)[Jimmy Gilmer and the Fireballs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Gilmer_and_the_Fireballs "Jimmy Gilmer and the Fireballs"), [The Ventures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ventures "The Ventures"), [Cliff Richard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cliff_Richard "Cliff Richard") and [the Shadows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Shadows "The Shadows"),[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Young#cite_note-31)[Chuck Berry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuck_Berry "Chuck Berry"), [Hank Marvin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hank_Marvin "Hank Marvin"), [Little Richard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Richard "Little Richard"), [Fats Domino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fats_Domino "Fats Domino"), [The Chantels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Chantels "The Chantels"), [The Monotones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Monotones The discography and filmography of Neil Young contains both albums and films produced by Young. Through his career most of Young's work has been recorded for and distributed by [Reprise Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reprise_Records "Reprise Records"), a company owned by [Warner Bros. Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Records "Warner Records") since 1963 and now part of the [Warner Music Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Music_Group "Warner Music Group"). The only exceptions are Young's five albums for [Geffen Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geffen_Records "Geffen Records") in the 1980s, which were once distributed by Warner, but are now distributed by [Universal Music Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Music_Group "Universal Music Group").
